title: Clinical Note Examples: One Therapy Visit in Four Formats
summary: Compare clinical note examples from one therapy visit in narrative, SOAP, DAP and BIRP formats. See what to keep when documenting the patient's response.
body_markdown:
A clinical note example shows how to document a behavioral health visit so another clinician can pick up where you left off. Useful clinical note examples distinguish what the patient reported from what you observed. They show how the patient responded to your intervention and what you plan to review together.


A full therapy note can bury the patient's response. A short one can leave it out. In either case, the next clinician has to guess what the patient could do independently.


Reconstructing a visit after hours takes work. Consider what you can leave out of this fictional follow-up while keeping enough detail for the next visit.

## What do three clinical note examples show about the same therapy visit?


Read each version as if you were about to see this patient. Look for the moment when the therapist could step back during rehearsal. Then look for what the patient hopes to do at work.


### What hides the response in an overlong note?


Fictional example: overlong narrative note


- Patient reported skipping the team meeting because of anxiety. Patient described the agenda: project updates first, then deadlines, then assignments. Patient wants to speak at the next meeting.
- Therapist asked how patient might start. Patient asked to hear an example. Therapist modeled an opening sentence about having a project update. Patient repeated the sentence after the therapist.
- Therapist took the role of meeting lead again. This time, patient used the opening sentence without prompting. Patient plans to try it at the next meeting. Therapist and patient will review the attempt next visit.


- **Cut:** The agenda tells you how the team runs a meeting. Its order changes nothing about the planned attempt.
- **Keep:** The patient's account of skipping the meeting explains why speaking at the next one matters.
- **Condense:** Keep the difference between repeating a sentence and using it without a cue. You can document that change without reconstructing the conversation.


### What does “engaged” leave out of a thin note?


Fictional example: thin narrative note


- Discussed work anxiety. Patient engaged. Continue therapy.


“Engaged” could describe someone who listened while the therapist modeled a sentence. It could also describe someone who used the sentence independently. “Continue therapy” leaves the next clinician without a specific attempt to ask about.


### What should stay in the revised narrative?


Fictional example: revised narrative progress note


- Patient reported skipping a team meeting because of anxiety and wants to speak at the next meeting.
- Therapist modeled an opening sentence. During rehearsal, patient used the sentence without prompting.
- Patient will try the opening sentence at the next meeting. Therapist and patient will review the attempt next visit.


The words “during rehearsal” keep the setting attached to the result. The therapist saw the patient begin speaking independently in session. Whether the same opening helps at work remains a question for follow-up.


## What clinical reasoning should survive a change in note format?


Start with what the patient wants to do: speak at the next team meeting. That goal explains why the therapist modeled an opening sentence. The patient's response tells you how much help the patient needed to begin after hearing the example.


### What links the goal to follow-up?


Following the goal through rehearsal to the planned workplace attempt illustrates[golden thread documentation](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/golden-thread-documentation) . Check that connection by reading backward from the plan. If the plan says the patient will try an opening sentence, can you find where the patient practiced it?


Use this prompt within a[behavioral health progress note template](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/progress-note-template) : “Patient reported __. To support __, clinician __. Patient __. Next visit, review __.” In the response field, describe what the patient could do and under what conditions.


## Where do the same facts go in SOAP?


Like other clinical note examples, this fictional[SOAP note example](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/soap-note-example) separates the patient's account from the therapist's observation. The assessment explains how far that observation supports a conclusion about progress. The plan identifies the workplace attempt the clinician and patient will review.


Fictional example: SOAP note


- **Subjective:** Patient reported skipping a team meeting because of anxiety. Patient wants to speak at the next one.
- **Objective:** Therapist modeled an opening sentence. Patient used the sentence without prompting during rehearsal.
- **Assessment:** Patient could start speaking independently during rehearsal. Patient reports that anxiety interferes with meeting participation and has yet to try the skill at work.
- **Plan:** Patient will try the opening sentence at the next meeting. Therapist and patient will review the attempt next visit.


Notice where the skipped meeting appears. The therapist heard about it from the patient, so it belongs under Subjective. The therapist witnessed the rehearsal and can document the patient's use of the opening sentence under Objective.


## How does the same visit look as a DAP or BIRP note?


A clinic might choose[DAP notes](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/dap-notes) when clinicians want the patient's report and session observations together under Data. Within that section, “patient reported” still tells the reader how the therapist learned about the missed meeting.


Fictional example: DAP note


- **Data:** Patient reported skipping a team meeting because of anxiety and wants to speak at the next one. Therapist modeled an opening sentence. Patient repeated it, then used it without prompting during rehearsal.
- **Assessment:** After modeling, patient could begin speaking independently in rehearsal. Patient has yet to try the opening sentence at work.
- **Plan:** Patient will try the opening sentence at the next team meeting. Therapist and patient will review the attempt next visit.


A clinic might choose[BIRP notes](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/birp-notes) when reviewers want to find the patient's response directly after the therapist's intervention. Here, modeling belongs under Intervention. What the patient did after hearing the model belongs under Response.


Fictional example: BIRP note


- **Behavior:** Patient reported skipping a team meeting because of anxiety. Patient wants to speak at the next meeting.
- **Intervention:** Therapist modeled an opening sentence about having a project update and took the role of meeting lead during rehearsal.
- **Response:** Patient first repeated the sentence after the therapist. During the next rehearsal, patient used the opening sentence without prompting.


Format Sections Best when


Narrative Free text without fixed headings A short account makes the sequence of care easy to follow.


SOAP Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan You want separate headings for patient report and clinician observation.


DAP Data, Assessment, Plan You want the reader to see the session details together before your assessment.


BIRP Behavior, Intervention, Response, Plan You want a dedicated place for the patient's response to the intervention.


## Which therapy details belong in the progress note?


Cutting the meeting agenda does not turn it into a psychotherapy note. A detail can have little value for follow-up without qualifying for special protection under HIPAA.


### What belongs in the shared progress note?


Document the independent rehearsal in the clinical record. It tells a covering clinician where to resume treatment. Without that detail, the clinician might spend the next visit establishing something the therapist already observed.


These fictional examples show different ways to document the same clinical work. Check your clinic's documentation requirements and your payer's rules before adopting a format.


### What qualifies as a separate psychotherapy note?


The HHS Office for Civil Rights defines[psychotherapy notes](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/2088/does-hipaa-provide-extra-protections-mental-health-information-compared-other-health-information/index.html) as a mental health professional's notes documenting or analyzing counseling conversations. The professional must maintain those notes separately from the rest of the medical record.


HIPAA excludes routine summaries of symptoms, progress, and treatment plans from that definition. A therapist's personal analysis of a counseling conversation may qualify when the therapist keeps it in separate[psychotherapy notes](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/psychotherapy-notes) . The meeting agenda alone gives the therapist no reason to create such a record.

## When should a supervisor return a progress note for revision?


Return “patient engaged” when it leaves you unable to tell what the patient practiced. Ask the writer whether the patient needed a prompt during rehearsal. That question identifies the missing observation without asking the writer to reconstruct the whole exchange.


### What omission warrants a rewrite?


Read the note as the clinician responsible for the next visit. Check whether you can answer each question from the note alone:


- **Goal:** What does the patient want to do at the next meeting?
- **Intervention:** What did the therapist model to support that goal?
- **Response:** Could the patient use the opening sentence without a prompt?
- **Next action:** Where will the patient try the skill, and when will the clinician review the attempt?


### When should reviewers accept different wording?


During onboarding, ask reviewers to mark missing details independently. Compare their decisions against the revised narrative. If reviewers disagree about the response, ask each to point to the words that tell them what the patient did.


Accept equivalent versions when both meet clinic and payer requirements. A request for the missing rehearsal result helps the next clinician. Moving that same result under a preferred heading adds little if the reader can already find and interpret it.


## What else do clinicians ask about progress notes?


What should I document if the patient practices a skill but reports no improvement yet?


Describe what you observed during practice, including any prompting the patient needed. Record the patient's report of no improvement separately. If the patient has yet to try the skill outside therapy, say that instead. Name the attempt you plan to review.


When does a patient's exact wording add more than a summary?


Quote the patient when their wording identifies a distinction that changes follow-up. If a summary conveys the same goal and the reason it matters, use the summary.


Should a supervisor return a note if the response appears under a different heading?


Accept the note if the response is clear and the format meets clinic and payer rules. Check whether the reader can distinguish the therapist's observation from the patient's account. Request a revision if the placement obscures that distinction.
